speechtext: Would a civil defence worker, or any other person participating in a civil defence scheme or trial be compensated if injured in the course of his or her duties?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Under agreements entered into by the federal government and the governments of Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan, a civil defence worker in those provinces, that is, any person duly enrolled and registered with the provincial director of civil defence for and while actually engaged in civil defence work, would be compensated for injury in the course of his or her civil defence duties. Persons not so registered would not receive compensation.
Negotiations directed toward execution of federal-provincial compensation agreements are at present under way with the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland.

speechtext: How much additional expenditure will the St. Lawrence seaway involve, (a) between lake Ontario and lake Erie; (b) between lake Erie and lake St. Clair; (c) between lake St. Clair and lake Huron; (d) between lake Huron and lake Superior, and who is responsible for the expenditure in each case?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUESTIONS
speechtext:
By the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act adopted in 1951, the St. Lawrence seaway
authority was incorporated for the purpose of constructing, operating and maintaining all such works as may be necessary to provide and maintain a deep waterway between the port of Montreal and lake Erie. Under present plans the authority expects to expend $2,000,000 between lake Ontario and lake Erie for further dredging in the Welland ship canal.
Though the channels between lake Erie and lake St. Clair, between lake St. Clair and lake Huron, and between lake Huron and lake Superior at present have controlling depths downbound of 25 feet and upbound of 21 feet the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act does not extend to those channels in which the dredging has in the past been done generally by the government of the United States. There is legislation pending before the congress of the United States to provide for deepening these channels to a depth of 27 feet.

speechtext: Will the minister indicate to the house what steps the government is taking to ensure an adequate supply of monkeys for the production and testing of the Salk vaccine?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The federal government has taken steps to assure a continuing supply of monkeys required in the production and testing of the Salk polio vaccine. Discussions have been held between officers of the departments of national health and welfare, trade and commerce, external affairs, and agriculture, and of the crown company, the Canadian Commercial Corporation.
Arrangements have now been worked out under which the Canadian Commercial Corporation will act as the purchasing agent for the government of Canada in obtaining monkeys under the terms of an export licence granted by the government of India. Monkeys required for the vaccine production programs

at the Connaught laboratories in Toronto and the institute of microbiology at Montreal, and for the safety testing of the vaccine at the federal laboratory of hygiene in Ottawa, will be bought in this way. The monkeys will, in turn, be purchased through the Canadian Commercial Corporation by the three laboratories concerned, with the cost per monkey pro-rated according to the total cost of the shipment.
This federal government action has been taken to ensure a continuing supply and to meet India's preference for dealing with one agency only. The government of India has been most co-operative in this whole matter.
Full precautions have been taken to safeguard the health of the animals while in transit and to ensure their humane treatment on arrival in Canada. All shipments will be met by veterinary inspectors. Monkeys procured under this arrangement will be used for no other purpose than in the production and testing of the Salk vaccine.
The first shipment of approximately 1,000 monkeys, purchased under the procedure described above, arrived at Malton airport on Monday, May 30.

Mr. Speaker, speaking in the debate yesterday the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said he could not support our amendment because he felt that if an independent commission were allowed to survey the operations of government and make recommendations for savings, it would in fact be an abdication by members of parliament of the responsibilities imposed upon us by those who sent us here. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said he felt this should be done by more thorough use of the committees of this house.
There is no doubt that a more thorough use could be made of house committees, and that

Government Services
expenditures proposed by the government should be thoroughly scrutinized by members of parliament. That is our primary responsibility; but I submit that unless an independent commission or an outside firm of recognized efficiency engineers is allowed to come in to survey the operations of this government and make recommendations for savings, then the operations of this government will not be streamlined and waste and extravagance will not be reduced.
I say that because of the way committees of this house operate. As we all know, every committee has a majority of government members. Take for example a committee examining the expenditures of a department, and they come to the item dealing with telephones and telegraphs. Quite naturally the members of the opposition object strongly to the outlandish expenditure on this account. The minister and the officials of the department defend their position; they say those expenditures are justified. The opposition asks more questions. The minister and the officials give answers of one kind or another. The opposition press their point that these expenditures are unwarranted. The minister and the departmental officials continue to defend their position. Then a motion to reduce the item is brought forward by the opposition; it is voted down by the government majority, the item is passed, and we go on to another item.
So every expenditure is passed by the government majority on the committee, not only for that department, but for every department of this government. I have been here for five years and I have known of only one reduction made in a vote in that time, and that was made only because the government admitted that there had been a bad calculation and agreed to change the vote on that account only.
The amount of taxes which the people of this country are paying unnecessarily every year on account of the inefficient operation of this government is very important indeed. I have risen on the second day of this debate to speak about it, because I feel very keenly about this matter. What we need is either an independent commission or a recognized firm of efficiency engineers to make a survey of the operations of this government and bring in recommendations for savings.
I should like to outline to the house how these efficiency engineers work. They come into a department and spend several weeks or several months, depending on the job to be tackled. They observe the operations of that department, and then discuss those operations with the personnel concerned. They find out why certain things are being

done, and how they are being done, and with their experience based on the training they have had in efficiency work, what they have seen of other industries and other similar operations, they do whatever they possibly can to figure out a better and cheaper method of carrying out the operation under scrutiny. At the end of the survey, they make recommendations on how they believe the operations of that department can be streamlined, and they outline specifically what savings could be effected.
Most successful businesses have periodic checks made on their operations by outside firms of efficiency engineers, because they know perfectly well that you cannot count on a department head to make a satisfactory efficiency check on his own department. It just is not human nature to expect a man to criticize his own department, because in effect he is then criticizing himself for allowing outworn systems to operate, and having inefficient personnel working for him.
These surveys usually produce very surprising results for the people who have them undertaken. Those engineers who come into a firm from the outside look on the operations of each department from a clear and unbiased point of view. They are often shocked by operations which appear to those who have worked in a department for a long time to be perfectly commonplace. In these surveys, savings of 10 per cent and more on operating expenses are the order of the day.
Now, let us realize that government is simply the biggest business in the country, and what applies to business with regard to improving efficiency of operation certainly applies to government. From what I have seen of the operations of this government, savings far in excess of 10 per cent of operating expenses could be effected. After all, this government has been operating for 20 years with unchecked inefficiency. Mr. Speaker, if this government had to operate as a business does, it would go bankrupt within six months. There is no doubt about that at all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the subamendment which is before the house at the present
Government Services
time I should like to emphasize that the Department of National Revenue is one of the most important departments of government. With this department not being operated in a proper manner other departments of government, especially those concerned with spending, would find their source of revenue dried up. I think on the whole the Department of National Revenue has a good record, but there have been times in Canadian history, and I think the present is such a time, when the people have been annoyed with the veil of secrecy drawn around this department. For more than a month hon. members of this house have been denied legitimate information which they should have as the elected representatives of the people.
It should be noted that a great many individuals and firms perform services for the government in the collecting and remitting to Ottawa of income and corporation taxes, without any compensation for such work. This places a real burden on Canadian business organizations and individuals. If we are to have the continued co-operation of all those performing collection services for the government then the government of Canada, particularly the Minister of National Revenue, must come clean and give a full and frank accounting of the operations of the department.
It is over 20 years since this department was in the public eye to the extent that it is at the moment. On February 5, 1926, the House of Commons adopted unanimously a resolution that a special committee of the house consisting of nine members be appointed forthwith to investigate the administration of the department of customs and excise, as it was then known, and the alleged serious losses to the public treasury because of inefficiency and corruption on the part of officers of the department and others. Later that year, on June 29, 1926, the special committee reported as follows:
Since the inquiry indicates that the smuggling evils are so extensive and their ramifications so far-reaching that only a portion of the illegal practices have been brought to light, your committee recommends the appointment of a judicial commission with full power to continue and complete investigating the administration of the department of customs and excise and to prosecute all offenders, and that such judicial commission should consist of a judge to be named by the two judges of the Exchequer Court of Canada, said judge acting as a commission, to have all the powers conferred upon such commission under the Public Inquiries Act. The said commission to have powers to make findings and recommendations and to report the same to parliament at the opening of the next session together with the evidence taken before the said commission.

Government Services
In answering a question of mine the Minister of National Revenue pointed out on Monday that the members of that commission were well known citizens. They were Hon. James Thomas Brown of Saskatchewan, who was the chairman; Hon. William Henry Wright, and Hon. Ernest Roy. Counsel were Hon. N. W. Rowell; Mr. R. L. Calder; Mr. R. B. Law and Mr. Gordon Lindsay. The cost of the commission was $375,716.65, but I think most Canadians will agree that the money was very well spent.
The commission reported certain information which certainly was disturbing, to say the least. At that time, as now, the government was insisting that there was nothing to worry about, that the department was above reproach. I find that there was a good deal of information regarding operations in my own part of the country. Apparently quite an extensive illegal liquor industry flourished. Reference was made to the Prairie Drug Company and Regina Wine and Spirit, Limited, which apparently did quite a sizeable business. They bottled, labelled and sold liquors on a wholesale scale without a licence, contrary to sections 187 and 196 of the Excise Act and in violation of the provisions of the Food and Drugs Act. They applied false trade marks and false descriptions to such goods. Those two companies apparently had receipts from sales from July, 1920, to December, 1921, of over $2 million.
Then reference was made to another group of companies. I am not going to mention any names, as I do not know how many of these people are still living. I am sure their names would be familiar to many people in western Canada. They operated Canada Drugs Limited, Yorkton Distributors, Dominion Distributors, Gainsborough Liquors Limited, Gainsborough Liquor Company, Atlas Shipping Company and Atlantic Import Company Limited. I might mention that I am reading from interim reports Nos. 1 to 10, royal commission on customs and excise. This document is marked confidential, but since it is found in the library of parliament and was produced as a result of the expenditure of over $375,000 I hope I am not running any risk in referring to it.
Canada Drugs Limited did a really worthwhile business. They imported from the United States about 300,000 gallons of alcohol, brought it to Yorkton, had it compounded and bottled and labelled the compound as Scotch whisky with labels not approved by the department according to the Excise Act, thus giving a false description of the contents therein.

Gainsborough Liquors Limited and Gainsborough Liquor Company also did quite a business. Both these companies were located in the constituency of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) but he would not be aware that 20 years ago two such influential companies operated in this small town of Gainsborough, near the United States border. The report states that it was alleged by Inspector Knowles-not the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-that on more than one occasion he had been offered a bribe to disregard his duties and desist from further interference with the operations of the firms or syndicates. This is to be found on page 54 of this report.
Then we have reference to Consolidated Distilleries Limited of Montreal and Wiser's Distillery Limited. The report states as follows:
The evidence shows that practically all of said goods were entered for export at customs and ostensibly shipped to points in Mexico and Central and South America but that the names of the consignees entered at customs were fictitious; that the liquors were not landed at the points designated in the export entries but, on the contrary, were largely disposed of off the coast of the United States to be smuggled into the United States and to some extent were apparently delivered off the coast of Canada and smuggled back into Canada.
The evidence also shows that false and fraudulent landing certificates were procured with reference to such goods and that such certificates were presented to customs and that on the strength of ruch certificates, the bonds of the respective distilleries were delivered up and cancelled.
I might mention that one of these two companies, Consolidated Distilleries Limited, owed $973,677.23, and Wiser's Distillery Limited owed $86,078.04.
I am sure that as a result of this royal commission the treasury of Canada benefited very substantially. I have no evidence whatever to indicate that these irregularities are being continued at the present time, but I submit that for the good of democracy and for the sake of the rights of this parliament the Prime Minister should ask for a free vote on this amendment which is before the house.
There are some things in connection with the operation of this department that certainly are not going to be produced to parliament but which would be produced to a commission such as we had in 1926. The questions asked by members on this side of the house since the 24th, 25th or 26th of April regarding the operations of this department of government, without having discussion, concern a matter which members of this house cannot accept without challenge.
I have a few clippings from newspapers. I am not going to mention them, but newspapers from coast to coast are disturbed

because the Prime Minister of Canada has refused to discuss the details which members of the opposition have insisted should be made public. The Minister of National Revenue remained silent when a few days ago the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked for photostatic copies of documents in the possession of the Department of National Revenue concerning advances or payments made or given by John T. Drohan, since deceased, to James Dempsey some time during the year 1951, which photostatic copies were shown by the Minister of National Revenue to the premier of Ontario on or about April 26 or 27 last.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is no good reason why a department of government cannot comply with such a reasonable request. In one of the two morning newspapers which reach us in time for breakfast I find that Arthur Blakely, commenting in "Ottawa Day by Day" says, "Reports current on parliament hill-"

But this year we intend to cover these estimates as thoroughly as we can, realizing at the same time the deficiency in examination which results from two things. The first of these is failure on the part of the government to answer. There was an example this afternoon of a question asked and unanswered, and which I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks. That is the kind of attitude we see on the part of the government-a refusal to answer ordinary and simple questions. The question I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) was this: Where did you get the photostatic copy? No answer has been given. It is not an answer requiring any knowledge of law.
Then, I ask other questions of various ministers, and invariably a similar type of answer is received, when it suits the minister in question to give that kind of answer.
In 1953, on the last day of the session, $150 million was voted. In 1952, we see, $100 million was voted on the last day, and in 1951 the amount of $200 million. The minister says, "Why do you not stay longer?" I say to him that I hope there will be a reorganization by the government of the manner in which it presents these estimates to parliament, so as to enable a fuller and more complete examination.
What did the Hoover commission do? Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition referred to some of its activities and some of the results of its work. We read in the New York Times of May 21 that Clarence Francis, chairman of the citizens' committee

for the Hoover report, a committee to which I intend to refer in a moment-
-predicted yesterday that if all its recommendations were promptly adopted the federal budget could be balanced overnight. He said also that its proposed elimination of waste and confusion in government could eventually reduce the national tax burden by 15 to 20 per cent.
Then he went on to deal with the first Hoover report of five years ago, and said:
The first Hoover report five years ago cost the government $2 million and has produced savings of at least $1,200 million a year in governmental economies.
That is not an estimate by some fly-bynight individual. That is the estimate of a man who is the chairman of this citizens' committee for the Hoover report. He sets out in detail the manner in which those savings had been effected.
Do not hon. members feel that an inquiry of the kind asked for here would have a good field in which to work, if it were to look into the printing bureau, this golden elephant that has been so many years in construction and, so far, has cost $12 million? Is that not a field for investigation, to determine the whys and the wherefors, the reasons why construction has taken so long, what work is being done, how much is being spent for machinery, and what the total cost will be, before the final completion? That is an example. Then there was another example in that massive building built by the mortgage corporation, the building with all the modern conveniences. Certainly the places that are to house institutions of parliament should be in keeping with the general surroundings. But luxuries such as that are unnecessary and unjustifiable at this time.
As the Leader of the Opposition said yesterday, the Hoover commission's aim was to promote economies, efficiency and improvement in the prosecution of the public business, and it recruited the task force to which the Leader of the Opposition referred, and which I shall not repeat at this time.
What did it find? It found in every department it examined that there were savings, great or small, that could be made. It found that there was waste, and that the waste was in the nature of Lilliputian threads that finally bound Gulliver, that destroyed efficiency in government. It found that there was red tape which undermined and overlapped departments, and that there was duplication which resulted in needless expense. All of this took place in the matter of a very few years.
So successful was this commission that was started during the time of the presidency of President Truman, a Democratic president,

that it was continued under President Eisenhower, and a second commission was set up.
Let me read some of the reports-and let me say I have read every one of them. There are a thousand pages of reports, and they are worth studying. It took a great deal of time to read them. In some instances, for one not trained in finance, they are difficult to understand. However, they do deal with subjects such as foreign affairs, national security organizations, labour, agriculture, finance, commerce, social security, public welfare, Indian affairs, the post office, independent regulatory commissions, transportation, and government in business. They point out the trend in the United States, one that is taking place here in Canada. They point out the ramifications of public enterprise to an extent that could never have been possible had it not been for two wars in one generation. They speak of it as creeping socialism. Having regard to the extent to which there has been an expansion in this country of public enterprise, in some cases in competition with private enterprise, we have achieved in this country galloping socialism, and within the last few years, through the establishment of government boards and public corporations.
The second commission which was set up in 1954 has given reports so far in 1955 on surplus property, food and clothing, lending agencies, federal medical services, personnel and civil service, legal procedure, business enterprises of government and natural resources. My hon. friends say that this would contradict the principles of parliamentary government. At the same time they say they intend to set up a commission that is to investigate Canada's economy 25 or 30 years from now. Let us have an inquiry such as is asked for by the hon. member for Greenwood in order to bring about savings. If they are even partially commensurate with those achieved by the Hoover commission in the United States they will run into hundreds of millions of dollars in the course of a year from now. But something more is needed than a Hoover commission, as they found in the United States. They set up the Hoover commission and it went to work on its task forces. Then, throughout the length and breadth of the United States, outstanding leaders in finance, in business, in agriculture, in the labour unions and in the fields of national research formed themselves into a non-profit organization in order to assist in the implementation of the Hoover report. In other words, what they said they wanted to do without regard to party or political considerations of any kind was to do away with the pork barrel 50433-273$

pressure groups and substitute the cracker barrel pressure groups of thrift in every part of the nation.
These people joined together and met regularly, and in the various states in which they lived they did their part to help the federal government resist the inroads of those who forever are demanding extra expenditures, thereby piling up an ever-increasing load of expenditures in the land. The citizens' committee for the Hoover report really put the United States back to school to study citizenship. I do not know how many of my hon. friends have read these reports, but from time to time they issue a book entitled "Status of the Hoover Report". It is published by the citizens' committee for the Hoover report, an organization of public-spirited Americans, who, in many communities in which they live, set up organizations to recommend to the government reductions in expenditures. Three hundred of these organizations have been set up in the United States. Through books, pamphlets, speeches, meetings and television, they have aroused the people in the United States to the need of a great effort in a great crusade to reduce unnecessary government expenditures. They were thanked by Mr. Hoover. Their motto is to make citizenship effective. In March, 1952, when he met them, Mr. Hoover said this:
You have given the nation about the widest education in civil government that it has had smce the constitution was under debate.
All over the United States there are groups of individuals who are constantly on the alert vigilantly recommending savings to be effected. Their slogan is: "Better government at a better price." I can think of no better slogan for Canadians today in a similar organization. Better government at a better price by bringing into effect within this country, under the leadership of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), and of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), similar organizations everywhere, which would bring about a state of mind on the part of the public against waste and extravagance, which would assure reductions of unnecessary expenditures and consequent reductions in taxation as well.
When the organization started in the United States, people said: "Oh, you cannot do that. After all, how are you going to mobilize the heart of the citizenry in the United States in behalf of something positive like that?" But they did. The recommendations -and I have a list of them here which are pages in length-have been carried into effect throughout the nation. When they started in they found the same attitude of cynicism. After all, people say, you cannot do this kind

Government Services
of thing, but that committee, after operating for two years, was able to say: We have helped to reverse the trend of cynicism, frustration and indifference with which far too many people were coming to regard the unbridled growth of big government. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) used the expression "big government" yesterday. This group of citizens in the United States, backed by the will of the government in power that was prepared to take assistance in the setting up of the non-partisan commission under former president Hoover, achieved what was believed to be impossible.
They are able to say today: In the first five years we have saved at the rate of $1,200 million a year; and those savings will be increased in the days ahead, because they believe that every dollar that is wasted is a gift to the enemies of freedom. They believe that a crusade such as they are carrying out will in the end do away with extravagance and waste. The experience of the Hoover commission can be pointed to as an example of what can be done elsewhere.
The Leader of the Opposition mentioned paper work. Well, we sometimes talk about red tape and governments having quadrupled work. Beyond that, I do not know what it is; it becomes governmental. But the fact remains that those investigators in the United States found that business was even worse in the keeping of unnecessary copies and the multiplication of duplications and triplications. As a result of the recommendations made in this one particular they found in 1954 that in the disposal of unnecessary documents the photostating of documents of government departments was sent to a central photostatic organization set up for the purpose. In 1954, $34,175,000 was saved on that one matter alone. I only hope that the experience of recent days indicates that this course is going to be followed by the government of Canada.
As far as letter writing is concerned, they found that it has multiplied per civil servant 9 times over what it was 43 years ago. They found that they could streamline correspondence. They found an effective saving in one office in Baltimore alone in that direction of $157,000 a year. They consolidated forms; they effected simplication. They did away with unnecessary records, and they say that when they are through with the organization they will in that one field save $250 million a year out of a total expenditure of some $4 billion.
Now, I suggest that on the basis of the experience in the United States this country
[Mr. Diefenbaker.I
is entitled to something more than a cavalier brush-aside of the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Greenwood.
Travelling expenses were mentioned. Well, we often talk about the money that we make on the Trans-Canada Air Lines. A year ago they had a surplus of $600,000. How many people realize that two years ago those who travelled from the armed forces on the T.C.A. had a larger expenditure than the surplus during the year? That is just one way of taking from one and handing to another. Certainly travelling expenses in the United States came down when travelling by those in authority in the armed forces, in the civil service, yes, in the government, found that that luxury was going to be examined and that unnecessary travelling, however interesting to the individual, was to be curtailed.
Then a word about paper work, and I am not going into the particulars in this connection. It was found that every filing cabinet of old documents that was retained cost $29 a year in office space. They were able to effect very large savings proportionately to the total expenditures by the means I mentioned a moment ago.
I do not intend to say more at this time. I rose to support the amendment of the hon. member for Greenwood and to ask the government whether it is not time to act and act effectively on a matter so necessary to the economic life of this nation. For as our taxes go up our industrial production finds itself unable to compete in the markets of the world. On that basis alone, aside from any other demands for economy, I ask the government to give consideration to the request that action be taken.
My hon. friend mentioned the publicity department. What should be done in the case of these publicity departments is to take an axe and just cut out most of what is being done. Instead of the torrents of adulation put out by publicity departments, it would save Canada millions if these bodies would simply say of the government: "Great is Diana of the Ephesians."

Mr. Speaker, in the space of a few minutes I want to say a few words on behalf of this group in connection with the request that has been made for an inquiry into the operation of one of the branches of this government. We do not believe that this is a proper approach to the question of the high cost of government. We do not feel that a single department should be made the target in an inquiry of this type.
On the other hand we believe that there is room for doubt as to whether or not the

business of this country is being handled efficiently. I think we all agree that the government of Canada is big business and in the operation of big business I submit that it is sound common sense and good business practice to examine periodically the conduct of such business for possible inefficiency.
We are not laying any charges against this government, but we do believe there is room for economy. We believe that this government is well aware of the fact that there is a growing feeling of alarm among the taxpayers of Canada that the costs of government are mounting so steadily. We would suggest that it would allay these fears if the conduct of the business of the government of Canada were investigated by a commission of experts. We believe that it would be a smart move on the part of this government to announce the appointment of such a commission and to lay before it the problem of bringing in a report on the conduct of the business of government and of crown companies and to make recommendations for economies that might be effected in government under good business practices.
If the government has nothing to hide it should welcome such an inquiry and if mis-practices are found by the commission they should be brought out in the open in the interests of Canadians.

When we tried to find out what the facts were, the veil of secrecy was thrown over us. Now the veil is moved slightly back, not by the government, not as the result of any opportunity that we are afforded here to obtain information, not because the government has decided that the opposition should have information of this nature, but because the Canadian Good Roads Association has made public correspondence in regard to this matter, and Canadians seeking accommodation in a Canadian hotel have to be told from New York whether we can hold conventions here in this country.
If there were no other single argument than this to demonstrate the need for an objective inquiry as to what is behind this veil of secrecy, this humiliating information that appears in the press today would suffice. We have handed over the control of our largest hotel, without any reason that holds

water being given, to a United States organization, which may be a very good organization in its own country but which certainly has nothing to do with Canadian standards or Canadian traditions or our desire to run Canadian hotels in a particular Canadian way. They are the people who not only provide the management but sit in judgment in New York on whether or not we can have accommodations. Of course, one cannot tell. Assume that the National Liberal Federation wanted to hold a convention in the Queen Elizabeth hotel. I wonder how they would like having to ask officials in New York whether the representatives of a party that they still regard as a great party could meet to carry on the ordinary functions of democracy in this country.
This is the kind of thing that will be brought out into the open and examined properly only when we have a task force of highly trained independent men and women who can perform in Canada the same kind of job that has been done so effectively in the United States. Exact figures cannot be given. We are told by such a responsible authority as the New York Times that savings to the extent of over $11 billion a year will be made as a result of the combined recommendations of the two Hoover commissions. I am not suggesting for one moment that on a proportionate basis we could effect a saving of over $1 billion a year, but I do say that, on the evidence and on all that we see, there is every reason to believe that the proposal we made for a saving of at least $500 million was indeed a very conservative estimate of what could be done. But there is more than the money saving involved. There is also the question of how these agencies carry on their business. There is also the question of how that fits into our private enterprise economy. There is also the question of whether we are going to sell out the Canadian agencies of government to those whose real interest is in another country, no matter how friendly that country may be.
I have placed this before the house to show why this inquiry should not be limited and why we will vote against the subamendment and why, when that subamendment is out of the way, I certainly hope that the amendment will be supported. If the government should take the rigid attitude that this should be dealt with only as a want of confidence motion, then may I express the hope that, dealing with this on a technical ground as a want of confidence motion, they will not close their ears, and above all their brains, to the compelling evidence we have before

us of the need for an efficient task force to examine the cost of government in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the question should be put and determined without the attention of the house and country being drawn to this further demonstration of the attitude of complete indifference on the part of the government to its responsibility toward parliament. I draw to your attention the fact that so far in this debate, which is now in its second day, not one spokesman for the government, not one government minister, has advanced any reason to the house or to his own colleagues, or indicated in any manner whatsoever, why the motion should not be accepted.
All we have had is a further indication of the attitude of the government that-"It is not necessary for us to say anything. All we have to do is to lay on the whip, and give no explanation to parliament. By the exercise of the whip, and by the dragooning of our party majority, we will defeat the motion, whatever its merits may be".
I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that, apart from one or two irrelevant and trivial interruptions made by private members, mostly

Government Services
on the government side-there have been only one or two interruptions made by ministers-there has been no statement by any member of the government, with the exception of that which is found at page 4295 of yesterday's Hansard where the Minister of Finance said:
If I may expedite the business of the house, I would point out to Your Honour that under no circumstances would the government entertain a motion by way of amending the supply motion as other than one of want of confidence.
He was there stating explicitly and clearly to the house and country that the government does not regard it as necessary to give any reasons for rejecting any motion made by the opposition or by anyone else in the house. He is simply saying, "We regard it as a vote of want of confidence. We therefore have to vote against it, whether there is merit in the motion or not". It is an example of an arrogant, autocratic and irresponsible government. It is another example of the way in which the government denies the very principles of responsible government.
This government, whether it realizes it or not, is responsible to the House of Commons. Here is a serious suggestion placed before the house by the official opposition, moved by the financial critic of the official opposition, a motion which most certainly demands from the government some explanation. Because, whether the minister realizes it or not, the people of this country are concerned over the steady increase in expenditures which has been the pattern during the term of office of this government. The people are concerned with the year-by-year increase of expenditures. The people are concerned to see that, as expenditures increase, by the same measure the sense of responsibility of the government appears to decrease.
I do not intend to detain the house very long, because it is not necessary to say much to demonstrate the complete irresponsibility and arrogance of the government. But what does concern me is the ready acquiescence of private members opposite, and their ready submission to the party whip, without a word of explanation from the ministers.
We have in this instance the Minister of Finance. Does the Minister of Finance really believe that the people of this country are-

speechtext: I was about to ask only a simple question, because the hon. member has referred to private members. I believe his reference entitles me to ask the question. Is it not possible that, after all, we voted the way we did because hon. members on the other side had not made a very good case?

I was prepared to hear that sort of thing from government ministers. However, I would point out that the hon. member has not yet voted on the amendment offered by the official opposition. It appears that he has made up his mind how he is going to vote, without even listening carefully to the arguments. But of course that is typical of what we find; that is typical of the attitude of mind of hon. members supporting the government.
My concern is mainly with members of the government. If it believes in the principle of responsible government and if it believes that it owes a duty to parliament to justify its measures and to justify its attitude in connection with important questions which are raised here, then I submit that it should demonstrate that sense of responsibility by giving some reasons as to why this amendment should be rejected.
I was saying a moment ago that the Minister of Finance, on whose motion this amendment is moved, is asking the House of Commons to go into committee of supply to authorize expenditures for this year. Are we to take it, from the silence of the Minister of Finance, that he believes the people of Canada are willing to vote him this money without any explanation from the government as to the efforts they will make or are making to reduce these expenditures and to keep them to a minimum?
The Minister of Finance has said nothing in the course of this debate; he has merely applied the party whip; he has said, we are not going to give you any explanation or any answer to your criticism or any justification or reason as to why your suggestion should be rejected. The Prime Minister is here. The Prime Minister, as leader of the government, exercises in his person the collective responsibility of his cabinet. I submit in all seriousness that he is under an obligation, either through himself or through one of his cabinet colleagues, to give some reason to the house, not just to the opposition, but to parliament itself, as to why this method of approach, why this commission of inquiry, which has been found to work to such good advantage elsewhere, should not be accepted in Canada.
I do not want to go into too much detail on the merit of the amendment. That has been adequately set out by my colleagues

who have already spoken; but I do point out that the government is not averse to the principle of royal commissions. Notwithstanding the fact that we have in Canada, in the government departments, a civil service of which we can be justly proud which has made and is making a constant study of the economic situation in this country, the government has not felt that it is a denial of the rights of parliament or of responsible government to move to set up a royal commission to survey the economic field in Canada and presumably to bring in recommendations upon which the government will be prepared to act. Because the suggestion comes from themselves, they regard that kind of commission as a proper, a constitutional move to make. Because this suggestion comes from the opposition for this type of commission of inquiry, then, judging by their attitude and by some of the things that were said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) last night, which drew applause from the government benches, it is somehow irresponsible and not worthy of consideration.
I suggest through you, sir, to the Prime Minister, and to the Minister of Finance, the people of Canada are not satisfied with the efforts being made by this government, because they see expenditures constantly increasing. If the government is itself unable to do anything to keep expenditures from increasing, then the people would, in my judgment, welcome a commission such as has been suggested, or would at least like to be told through their representatives in parliament why the government feels that such a commission would not produce beneficial results.
The Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Revenue are here. One can understand why the last mentioned hon. gentleman might be somewhat reluctant to advance any views at the present time, but nevertheless he is there exercising his share of responsibility. It is most unusual for the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration not to expound his views to the house as to why this suggestion should not be entertained. I can assure the minister that at this time we would be willing to hear from him if he entertains with respect to parliament that sense of responsibility which on other occasions elsewhere he has been so free to indicate he has.
Then, there is the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler). Has he nothing to say in regard to this matter? Certainly, the organization for which he answers to parliament, namely, the Canadian National Railways, spends a lot of the people's money. There 50433-274

The house resumed, from Wednesday, May 18, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Pinard-Mr. Applewhaite in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Canada Elections Act including provision for an increase in the salary of the chief electoral officer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think it would be appropriate at this point to raise a question in regard to a change that has been made in the act, about which I am sure there is a very real difference of opinion. That is the introduction into the act of a provision that nomination day would be three weeks ahead of election day. There are many very obvious reasons why two weeks is adequate. I would hope that the government would indicate that it would support the change to two weeks instead of three, because that has been our practice for some time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

The bill was introduced in the form in which it was reported from the committee, but we have ascertained that there was little consideration to that problem in the committee, and we did not want to

bring in a bill that differed from that recommended by the committee. If it is the desire of the house-I know it is the desire of a large number on this side of the house- that the delay remain at two weeks as it has been heretofore, the government will leave it to the free vote of all members of the house if the suggestion is made that the former delay of two weeks be continued in the amended bill.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext: I am very glad to hear the Prime Minister say what he has said, though I was prepared to speak in favour of the retention of the 14-day period as it was in the old act. I do not like section 8 in this amendment of the bill and I certainly give my support to the 14-day period rather than the 21-day period as it is in section 8 of the bill.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is unfortunately not here; he is in Winnipeg in connection with some celebration. The last time this matter was before the house he had some interesting comments to make regarding the filing of election expenses required by law after the election is over. I wonder if the minister could make some comment at this stage, keeping in mind the suggestions made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, indicating whether or not he will be prepared to include in the new act some amendments to the current legislation so that all the candidates in all constituencies of Canada would file returns and that these returns would be made available here, so that some department of government would be responsible for enforcing the law. I notice that among those who failed to report their expenses were several former members of parliament who should not have any excuse for not knowing the law. There were some barristers at law who should not have the excuse that they did not have the necessary education to complete these forms, which are not too complicated.

speechtext:
In so far as the suggestion made by my hon. friend is concerned, I would think that this matter should have been submitted to the committee itself, when the question of expenses of candidates came up for discussion. The only change suggested to the act was in section 17 of the act, to increase from $1,000 to $2,000 the amount of expenses allowed to a candidate to be spent by him. It would have been possible at the appropriate time to discuss also the problem to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre gave his attention the other day. In so far as the other suggestion is concerned, as to finding ways and means of forcing candidates, either defeated or elected, to file their returns, I should have thoughl that this matter also could have been studied better before a committee which is charged with revising the whole act. I do not think that it would be appropriate for the minister -who in this case is simply the spokesman of the chief electoral officer, and is not to direct his actions-to make a suggestion that the act be amended according to the views expressed. I would much prefer to see such a question fully discussed in committee and that suggestions be made by my hon. friend and by all those who, like him and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, hold strong views in that respect. A study by a committee of that question would possibly allow of a better way of putting into effect this suggestion to force candidates to file their election returns, and, if they did not do so, be subject to a penalty.
On the whole I would simply say this. I think it is not an appropriate function of the government to express strong views on matters that affect the conduct of elections. This is a matter that belongs not to a department of government but to every member of

Canada Elections Act
this house; and in my opinion it is more appropriate that questions of that nature be studied in committee so that representatives of all parties may express their views and, in doing so, may have the assistance of the chief electoral officer so as to allow the act to be amended in such a way as to serve ihe interests of all Canadians.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
